With a liveliness that went beyond the usual eagerness of a nature never indifferent to doing everything well and attentively, and with the genuine goodwill of a mind pleased with its own thoughts, she then performed all the duties of the meal, offering and praising the minced chicken and scalloped oysters with a warmth she knew would please the early hours and polite scruples of their guests.

On such evenings, poor Mr. Woodhouse was in great internal conflict. He had a fondness for the cloth being laid, as it had been in his youth, but his belief that suppers were very unwholesome made him regret seeing anything placed upon it; and while his hospitality would have welcomed his guests to everything, his concern for their health made him sorrowful that they would eat.

A small bowl of thin gruel like his own was all he could recommend with complete satisfaction; though he might manage, while the ladies were comfortably finishing the more delicate dishes, to say:

“Mrs. Bates, let me suggest you try one of these eggs. An egg boiled very softly is not unhealthy. Serle understands boiling eggs better than anyone. I would not recommend an egg boiled by anyone else; but you need not worry, they are very small, you see—one of our small eggs will not harm you. Miss Bates, let Emma assist you with a little piece of tart—a very little piece. Ours are all apple tarts. You need not fear unhealthy preserves here. I do not advise the custard. Mrs. Goddard, what say you to half a glass of wine? A small half-glass, poured into a tumbler of water? I do not think it could disagree with you.”

Emma allowed her father to speak—but she provided her guests in a much more satisfying manner, and on the present evening had particular pleasure in sending them away happy. The happiness of Miss Smith was quite equal to her intentions. Miss Woodhouse was such an important figure in Highbury, that the expectation of the introduction had given as much alarm as delight; but the modest, grateful little girl left with feelings greatly pleased, delighted with the kindness with which Miss Woodhouse had treated her all evening, and actually shook hands with her at last!

{  "passage_id": "AUSTEN_EMMA_002",
  "condition": "paraphrase",
  "rewritten_text": "The list she compiled when she was just fourteen—I recall being so impressed by her discernment that I kept it for a while; and I daresay she has produced an even better one now. But I have given up on expecting Emma to follow any regular course of reading. She will never submit to anything that demands diligence and perseverance, or that requires the imagination to yield to reason. Where Miss Taylor failed to inspire, I can confidently say that Harriet Smith will achieve nothing.—You could never persuade her to read as much as you desired.—You know you could not.”

“‘I dare say,’ replied Mrs. Weston, with a smile, ‘that I thought so _then_;—but since we have parted, I can never recall Emma failing to do anything I wished.’”

“There is little point in trying to revive such a memory as _that_,” said Mr. Knightley, feelingly; and for a moment or two he was silent. “But I,” he soon added, “who have had no such enchantment over my senses, must still see, hear, and remember. Emma is spoiled by being the cleverest in her family. At ten years old, she had the misfortune of being able to answer questions that baffled her sister at seventeen. She was always quick and confident: Isabella slow and uncertain. And ever since she was twelve, Emma has ruled the household and all of you. In her mother, she lost the only person capable of managing her. She inherits her mother’s talents, and must have been under her control.”

“I should have been sorry, Mr. Knightley, to rely on _your_ recommendation, had I left Mr. Woodhouse’s family and needed another position; I do not think you would have spoken kindly of me to anyone. I am certain you always thought me unfit for the role I held.”

“Yes,” he said, smiling. “You are better suited _here_; very fit for a wife, but not at all for a governess. But you were preparing yourself to be an excellent wife all the time you were at Hartfield. You might not have given Emma the thorough education your abilities seemed to promise; but you were receiving a very good education from _her_, on the essential matrimonial matter of yielding your own will, and doing as you were told; and if Weston had asked me to recommend him a wife, I should certainly have named Miss Taylor.”

“Thank you. There will be very little merit in making a good wife to such a man as Mr. Weston.”

“Why, to be honest, I am afraid you are rather wasted, and that with every inclination to endure, there will be nothing to endure. We will not despair, however. Weston may grow cross from the indulgence of ease, or his son may plague him.”

“I hope not _that_.—It is not likely. No, Mr. Knightley, do not predict trouble from that quarter.”

“Not I, indeed. I only mention possibilities. I do not claim Emma’s genius for predicting and guessing. I hope, with all my heart, the young man may be a Weston in merit, and a Churchill in fortune.—But Harriet Smith—I have not half finished speaking of Harriet Smith. I think her the very worst sort of companion that Emma could possibly have."
}

{  "passage_id": "AUSTEN_EMMA_004",
  "condition": "paraphrase",
  "rewritten_text": "And is she, at seventeen, just beginning life, just starting to be noticed, to be admired for not accepting the first proposal she receives? No—pray allow her time to consider her options.”

“I have always considered it a foolish attachment,” Mr. Knightley remarked after a moment, “though I have kept my thoughts to myself; but I now see it will be a regrettable one for Harriet. You will inflate her with notions of her own beauty and of what she is entitled to, until in a short time no one within her reach will seem good enough for her. Pride, when it takes hold of a weak mind, brings about all sorts of trouble. It is so easy for a young lady to expect too much. Miss Harriet Smith may not find proposals of marriage coming in so quickly, though she is a very pretty girl. Men of sense, whatever you may choose to say, do not seek foolish wives. Men of standing would not be particularly eager to link themselves with a girl of such uncertain background—and the most prudent men would be wary of the inconvenience and disgrace they might face when the mystery of her parentage is uncovered. Let her marry Robert Martin, and she is safe, respected, and happy for ever; but if you encourage her to hope for a grander match, and teach her to accept nothing less than a man of importance and considerable fortune, she may end up as a parlour-boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s for the rest of her life—or, at the very least, (for Harriet Smith is a girl who will marry someone or other,) until she becomes desperate and is glad to accept the son of the old writing-master.”

“You and I differ so greatly on this matter, Mr. Knightley, that there is no point in arguing. We shall only make each other more vexed. But as for my _allowing_ her to marry Robert Martin, it is impossible; she has refused him, and so firmly, I think, as must prevent any further attempt. She must suffer the consequences of having refused him, whatever they may be; and as for the refusal itself, I will not pretend to say that I might not have had some influence; but I assure you there was very little for me or anyone else to do. His appearance is so much against him, and his manner so poor, that if she ever were inclined to favor him, she is not now. I can imagine that before she had met anyone better, she might have tolerated him. He was the brother of her friends, and he made an effort to please her; and altogether, having seen nobody more refined (that must have been his great advantage) she might not, while she was at Abbey-Mill, have found him disagreeable. But the situation is different now. She knows what gentlemen are; and nothing but a gentleman in education and manner has any chance with Harriet.”

“Fiddlesticks, absurd fiddlesticks, as ever was said!” exclaimed Mr. Knightley.—“Robert Martin’s manner has sense, sincerity, and good humour to recommend it; and his mind has more true gentility than Harriet Smith could understand.”

Emma said nothing, and tried to appear cheerful and unconcerned, but was truly feeling uneasy and wished him very much to leave."
}

Miss Harriet Smith might not find marriage proposals coming in as fast as she’d like, even though she’s a very pretty girl. Sensible men, no matter what you might say, don’t want silly wives. Men with good families wouldn’t be too keen on linking up with a girl of such uncertain background—and most careful men would be worried about the trouble and embarrassment they might get into when the mystery of her parentage comes out. "We see this issue so differently, Mr. Knightley, that there’s no point in arguing. We’ll just end up more annoyed with each other. But as for my _letting_ her marry Robert Martin, it’s impossible; she refused him, and so firmly, I think, that he won’t try again. She has to live with the consequences of her refusal, whatever they are; and as for the refusal itself, I won’t pretend I might have had some influence over her; but I assure you there wasn’t much for me or anyone else to do. I can imagine that before she met anyone better, she might have put up with him. {  "passage_id": "AUSTEN_EMMA_018",
  "condition": "paraphrase",
  "rewritten_text": "The full measure of your admiration might one day surprise you.

Mr. Knightley was busily fastening the lower buttons of his heavy leather gaiters, and either the effort of doing so or some other cause brought a flush to his face as he replied,

“Oh! are you there?—But you are far behind. Mr. Cole gave me a hint of it six weeks ago.”

He paused.—Emma felt her foot touched by Mrs. Weston and was unsure how to interpret it. In a moment he continued—

“That will never happen, however, I can assure you. Miss Fairfax, I daresay, would not have me if I were to propose—and I am quite certain I shall never ask her.”

Emma responded to her friend’s gesture with warmth; she was pleased enough to say,

“You are not conceited, Mr. Knightley. I will say that for you.”

He appeared scarcely to hear her; he was deep in thought—and soon, in a manner that showed he was not pleased, remarked,

“So you have been deciding that I should marry Jane Fairfax?”

“No indeed I have not. You have scolded me too often for matchmaking for me to presume to take such a liberty with you. What I said just now meant nothing. One says those sorts of things naturally, without any serious intent. Oh! no, I assure you, I have not the slightest desire for you to marry Jane Fairfax or any other Jane. You would not be joining us in such a comfortable way if you were married.”

Mr. Knightley fell into thought again. The result of his musings was, “No, Emma, I do not think the full measure of my admiration for her will ever surprise me.—I have never had any such feelings for her, I assure you.” And shortly after, “Jane Fairfax is a very agreeable young woman—but not even Jane Fairfax is without flaw. She has a fault. She lacks the openness of character which a man would wish for in a wife.”

Emma could not help but be glad to hear that she had a fault. “Well,” she said, “and you soon silenced Mr. Cole, I suppose?”

“Yes, very soon. He gave me a quiet suggestion; I told him he was mistaken; he apologized and said no more. Cole does not wish to be wiser or cleverer than his neighbors.”

“In that respect how unlike dear Mrs. Elton, who wishes to be wiser and cleverer than the whole world! I wonder how she speaks of the Coles—what she calls them! How can she find a name for them, sufficiently vulgar in tone? She calls you, Knightley—what can she do for Mr. Cole? And so I am not surprised that Jane Fairfax accepts her civilities and agrees to be with her. Mrs. Weston, your reasoning carries most weight with me. I can much more easily understand the temptation of escaping from Miss Bates than I can believe in Miss Fairfax’s mind triumphing over Mrs. Elton. I have no confidence in Mrs. Elton’s acknowledging herself inferior in thought, word, or deed; or in her being restrained beyond her limited sense of good manners. I cannot imagine that she will not constantly be flattering her guest with praise, encouragement, and offers of assistance; that she will not constantly be recounting her grand plans, from securing her a permanent position to including her in those delightful excursions which are to take place in the barouche-landau.”
}

  "condition": "paraphrase",
  "rewritten_text": "I hurried along here as fast as I could, and had just crossed a ditch I knew was close to the Battery, and had just climbed up the bank beyond it, when I spotted the man sitting in front of me. I thought he would be more pleased if I surprised him with his breakfast, so I crept forward and gently touched his shoulder. He immediately jumped up, but it was not the same man, but a different one!

And yet this man was also dressed in coarse grey, had a heavy iron on his leg, was limping, hoarse, and cold, and shared all the other traits of the first man; except for his face, and he wore a flat, wide-brimmed, low-crowned felt hat. I saw all this in an instant, for I had only a moment to take it in: he cursed at me, swung at me—it was a feeble round blow that missed me and nearly knocked himself over, for it made him stumble—and then he ran into the fog, stumbling twice as he went, and I lost sight of him.

'It’s the young man!' I thought, my heart leaping as I recognized him. I suppose I would have felt a pain in my liver too, if I had known where it was.

I soon reached the Battery after that, and there was the correct man—hugging himself and limping back and forth, as if he had never stopped hugging and limping all night—waiting for me. He was dreadfully cold, to be sure. I half expected to see him collapse before my eyes and die from the bitter cold. His eyes looked so dreadfully hungry too, that when I gave him the file and he placed it on the grass, it occurred to me he might have tried to eat it, if he had not noticed my bundle. He did not turn me upside down this time to get at what I had, but left me upright while I opened the bundle and emptied my pockets.

'What's in the bottle, boy?' he asked.

'Brandy,' I replied.

He was already shoving mincemeat down his throat in the most peculiar way—more like a man trying to store it away somewhere in a great rush, than a man eating it—but he paused to take some of the drink. He shivered so violently all the while, that it was quite a struggle for him to keep the bottle's neck between his teeth, without biting it off.

'I think you have the ague,' I said.

'I agree with you, boy,' he said.

'It’s bad in this place,' I told him. 'You’ve been lying out on the meshes, and they’re dreadful for causing ague. They’re rheumatic too.'

We differ from Mr. Poe in our views on the aims of art. He believes the goal is the creation of Beauty, and it may be only in the interpretation of that term that we find ourselves at odds. In our remarks on his writings, however, we shall follow his own standard as our guide. The sanctuary of the muse is open from every direction, and there is ample space within it for all who offer tribute or seek prophecy.

In his stories, Mr. Poe has chosen to demonstrate his talent primarily in that shadowy realm that lies at the edge of the plausible and stretches into the strange boundaries of superstition and the unreal. He possesses a striking ability to blend two faculties rarely found together: the capacity to affect the reader's mind with the subtle suggestions of mystery and an attention to detail so thorough that not even a pin or a button escapes notice. Both traits stem naturally from the dominant feature of his intellect, which we have previously mentioned—analysis. This is what sets the artist apart. His mind immediately grasps the desired effect. Once he has decided to evoke certain feelings in the reader, he ensures that every element contributes precisely to the central aim. Even his mystery is calculated in his mind. To him, X is a known variable throughout. In any scene he creates, he understands the chemical nature of all his colors. Although some of his figures may appear indistinct, and the shadows formless, to him the contours are as clear and defined as those of a geometric figure. For this reason, Mr. Poe has no affinity for Mysticism. The Mystic lives within the mystery, is wrapped in it; it tinges all his thoughts; it especially affects his vision, and the most ordinary things acquire a prismatic glow from it. Mr. Poe, by contrast, is an observer from the outside. He examines, he dissects, he watches

“with an eye serene,
The very pulse of the machine,”

for it is essentially a machine to him, with gears and cogs and piston-rods, all working to achieve a specific outcome.

This analytical nature of his mind tempers the poetic, and by giving him the endurance to be meticulous, allows him to inject a remarkable sense of reality into his most fantastical ideas. A monomania he portrays with great strength. He enjoys dissecting one of these mental tumors and tracing all the delicate extensions of its roots. In conjuring images of horror, too, he achieves unusual success, sometimes conveying to us by a faint suggestion some dreadful uncertainty, which is the essence of all horror. He leaves the imagination the task of completing the picture, a task to which only it is suited.

“For much imaginary work was there;
Conceit deceitful, so compact, so kind,
That for Achilles’ image stood his spear
Grasped in an armed hand; himself behind
Was left unseen, save to the eye of mind.”
